evidence_excerpts: The weight of evidence suggests that alpha-band oscillations can be actively invoked within cortical regions across multiple sensory systems, particularly when these regions are involved in processing irrelevant or distracting information.
We have described evidence for alpha-band oscillations as a mechanism for attentionally mediated selective suppression of distracting information.
claims.text: Alpha-band oscillations in the 8-14 Hz range operate as an attentional suppression mechanism when sensory objects, features, or locations must be ignored.

evidence_excerpts: In contrast, an instructional cuing paradigm requires the participants to respond to targets occurring at the cued location only, and to ignore the uncued location completely. In this way, the uncued location becomes simply a source of potentially distracting information.
claims.text: Instructional cuing paradigms isolate suppressive attention because uncued locations or modalities become sources of distracter information rather than alternative targets.

evidence_excerpts: The cue instruction to attend the auditory modality (the word 'BEEP') resulted in significantly larger 8-14 Hz activity over parieto-occipital cortex in the anticipatory period preceding the S2 than when subjects were cued to attend the visual modality (the word 'FLASH').
The fundamental finding of Foxe et al. (1998) - increases in parieto-occipital alpha power in preparation for the auditory task - was replicated.
claims.text: During intersensory attention, preparing for an auditory task produces larger parieto-occipital alpha activity than preparing for a visual task, consistent with visual gating.

evidence_excerpts: A sustained divergence in TSE amplitude is seen starting at approximately 500 ms, which depends on both the cued direction of attention and the side of recording. TSE amplitudes are larger over occipital cortex ipsilateral to the direction of attention.

Enhanced alpha-band activity was seen over the retinotopic area that was likely to contain distracter stimuli, consistent with a role for these oscillatory processes in inhibition of non-cued spatial locations.
claims.text: Visual spatial attention increases alpha activity over occipital cortex ipsilateral to the attended direction, placing stronger alpha over retinotopic regions likely to receive distracters.

evidence_excerpts: Such sources located in putative dorsal stream regions showed increased power in the alpha band when motion was irrelevant, whereas sources located in ventral regions showed increased alpha power when color was irrelevant.

Components with higher alpha power for attention to color are generally localized to putative dorsal visual stream regions, whereas components with higher alpha power for attention to motion are generally localized to putative ventral visual stream regions.
claims.text: Feature-based visual attention increases alpha power in cortical streams that process the currently irrelevant feature.

evidence_excerpts: They found alpha-band increases over parietal cortex ipsilateral to the cued direction, consistent with the findings of Worden et al. (2000).

In these tactile attention experiments, alpha band increases are typically observed over somatosensory cortex ipsilateral to the cued direction, suggesting some degree of sensory specificity to the mechanism.
claims.text: Alpha-mediated biasing extends beyond vision into auditory and somatosensory spatial attention, where alpha increases appear over cortices ipsilateral to the cued direction.

evidence_excerpts: The key result was that, following the cue, alpha power ipsilateral to the cued direction increased above pre-cue baseline levels, and no decreases in alpha power contralateral to the cued direction were observed.

Because bilateral stimulation continued throughout each trial, we concluded that such increases in alpha power reflect active suppression of the to-be-ignored stimulus stream, rather than a mere return to baseline 'idling.'
claims.text: Alpha increases during selective attention reflect active suppression rather than merely a passive return to cortical idling baseline.

evidence_excerpts: Detection and discrimination of centrally presented near-threshold visual stimuli have been shown to be inversely related to the amplitude of alpha preceding stimulus onset.

Phosphene threshold was positively correlated with resting power in the alpha band across individuals. That is, more intense stimulation was required to evoke visual percepts in individuals with greater alpha levels.
claims.text: Higher pre-stimulus alpha power predicts reduced visual excitability and poorer near-threshold perceptual performance.

evidence_excerpts: TMS at 10 Hz impaired visual detection contralateral to the site of stimulation for both occipital and parietal stimulation sites, consistent with a spatially specific suppressive role of alpha-band activity with a cortical origin.
Critically, no effects on visual detection were seen for stimulation at either 5 or 20 Hz.
claims.text: Externally driving occipital or parietal cortex at 10 Hz causally impairs contralateral visual detection and improves ipsilateral detection, whereas 5 Hz and 20 Hz stimulation do not produce the same effect.

evidence_excerpts: These results strongly implicate the involvement of a fronto-parietal attention control network in the deployment of alpha-mediated gating mechanisms in visual cortex.

The strongest evidence from human TMS studies and monkey intracranial recordings indicates that attention-related alpha modulations are predominately under the control of a cortico-cortical network involving frontal and parietal regions, with a possible secondary influence from thalamo-cortical connections.
claims.text: Attention-related alpha modulation is likely controlled primarily by a cortico-cortical fronto-parietal network with possible secondary thalamo-cortical influence.

evidence_items.excerpt: Participants viewed a cue word (BEEP or FLASH) before a compound audio-visual target. Band-pass filtered 8-14 Hz waveforms revealed greater alpha activity in the 300 ms before target onset when attention was cued to the auditory modality; the text reports significantly larger 8-14 Hz activity over parieto-occipital cortex for BEEP than FLASH cues.
evidence_items.overview: This intersensory cueing result supplies a concrete EEG pattern for the review's gating hypothesis. When vision is task-irrelevant and audition is relevant, parieto-occipital alpha rises before the target arrives, matching the prediction that visual cortex can be pre-emptively suppressed. The effect is bounded by the original task design and supports anticipatory gating rather than a direct measurement of single-neuron inhibition.
evidence_items.title: Auditory Cue Alpha Increase

evidence_items.excerpt: In the visuo-spatial cueing experiment, alpha-band TSE amplitudes were larger over occipital cortex ipsilateral to the direction of attention, with sustained divergence beginning around 500 ms. The review states that enhanced alpha occurred over the retinotopic area likely to contain distracter stimuli and moved with upper or lower quadrant attention.
evidence_items.overview: The retinotopic pattern is important because it links alpha power to the sensory map of ignored space rather than to a global arousal state. Alpha rises where distracters are expected, not simply everywhere, making the suppressive interpretation more anatomically specific. The cited finding remains a scalp-level EEG inference and is strongest as converging evidence with later replications.
evidence_items.title: Retinotopic Spatial Alpha

evidence_items.excerpt: Independent components analysis isolated alpha-reactive components during the preparatory cue-target interval. Dorsal visual stream sources showed increased alpha power when motion was irrelevant, whereas ventral stream sources showed increased alpha power when color was irrelevant; component source distributions for the two feature sensitivities were significantly different.
evidence_items.overview: This evidence extends alpha suppression beyond spatial orienting. Because color and motion have different cortical processing streams, alpha increases in the stream tied to the irrelevant feature support a feature-selective gating account. The finding depends on ICA source estimation and is therefore best interpreted as source-localized EEG evidence rather than direct cortical recording.
evidence_items.title: Feature Stream Alpha Dissociation

evidence_items.excerpt: With rapid streams of letters presented to both visual hemifields, a central cue instructed participants to attend one stream and count target letters. Following the cue, alpha power ipsilateral to the cued direction increased above pre-cue baseline, with no contralateral decreases, while bilateral stimulation continued throughout each trial.
evidence_items.overview: This design directly addresses the idling alternative. Because visual stimulation remains present bilaterally, an alpha increase above baseline over the ignored stream is harder to explain as a passive rebound after stimulus offset. It supports active suppression of the to-be-ignored stream, while still leaving open whether the suppression acts at early sensory, later attentional, or multiple processing levels.
evidence_items.title: Bilateral RSVP Suppression Test

evidence_items.excerpt: The review reports that detection and discrimination of near-threshold visual stimuli are inversely related to pre-stimulus alpha amplitude, and that participants with greater tonic alpha levels in a sustained-attention task had larger LP1 components, with that relationship predicting task performance.
evidence_items.overview: Performance correlations make the alpha pattern behaviorally consequential. The evidence indicates that alpha level is not merely an electrophysiological by-product; it tracks perceptual sensitivity and attentional success. These are correlational findings, so they establish prediction and functional relevance but require causal manipulation for stronger mechanistic inference.
evidence_items.title: Alpha Predicts Performance

evidence_items.excerpt: Rhythmic TMS pulses were applied at 10 Hz, 20 Hz, or 5 Hz to occipital and parietal regions while participants reported near-threshold visual stimuli. Ten hertz TMS impaired visual detection contralateral to stimulation and improved ipsilateral detection; no visual detection effects were observed for 5 Hz or 20 Hz stimulation.
evidence_items.overview: The rhythmic TMS result is the review's clearest causal evidence. Driving cortex at an alpha-band frequency selectively changes perception in the predicted spatial direction, strengthening the interpretation that alpha oscillations can suppress sensory processing. Its scope is restricted to short-lived externally induced effects and does not by itself specify the full circuit mechanism.
evidence_items.title: Ten Hertz TMS Effect

evidence_items.excerpt: In a visuo-spatial attention task, TMS to IPS or FEF, but not pre-central gyrus, reduced typical anticipatory alpha decreases; IPS stimulation produced anticipatory increases. The degree of TMS disruption of alpha decreases was related to participants' response speed to targets.
evidence_items.overview: This evidence connects alpha gating to control regions rather than only to sensory cortex. Perturbing IPS and FEF changes anticipatory alpha dynamics and behavior, supporting a fronto-parietal mechanism for deploying alpha-mediated gating. Because the task differed from classic distracter-only designs, the result is best read as control-network evidence, not as proof that every alpha effect has the same spatial form.
evidence_items.title: Fronto-Parietal Control Evidence

evidence_items.excerpt: Bollimunta et al. recorded differential voltages across the approximately 2 mm cortical mantle with a 14-electrode linear array in alert monkeys. In areas V2 and V4, infragranular layers served as local alpha pacemakers with small granular influence; alpha power in V2 and V4 showed strong negative correlations with task performance.
evidence_items.overview: The monkey laminar evidence supplies anatomical depth missing from scalp EEG. Local pacemaker patterns and performance correlations in V2/V4 are consistent with cortico-cortical feedback and suppression of competing visual information. The review also notes that IT showed a different positive correlation, so alpha is not treated as a unitary rhythm across cortical areas.
evidence_items.title: Monkey Laminar Alpha

relations.rationale: Intersensory alpha increases provide one concrete case of the general sensory-suppression claim.
Retinotopic alpha over ignored visual space supports alpha as selective distracter suppression.
The baseline-controlled bilateral RSVP result supports active rather than passive alpha suppression.
Circuit evidence constrains the general mechanism to cortico-cortical and possible thalamo-cortical control pathways.

source.article_title: The role of alpha-band brain oscillations as a sensory suppression mechanism during selective attention
source.display_title: Alpha Oscillations Suppress Distracting Sensory Input

source_date_inference.rationale: The extracted first page explicitly states 'published: 05 July 2011' beside the review article metadata.

sections.body: The source's core proposition is that alpha-band oscillations can be deliberately recruited to suppress sensory channels, spatial locations, or features that conflict with current goals. Rather than treating alpha as a generic idling rhythm, the review frames alpha as a top-down attentional gate whose power increases where distracting information is expected.
sections.heading: Central Argument

sections.body: The review relies heavily on instructional cueing because it makes the unattended input behaviorally irrelevant. This matters methodologically: in probabilistic cueing, uncued targets may still require responses, but in instructional paradigms uncued input can be interpreted as distraction, so anticipatory alpha over that input's cortical representation is meaningful evidence for suppression.
sections.heading: Cueing Logic

sections.body: Visual spatial findings show alpha increases over occipital cortex ipsilateral to attention, corresponding to retinotopic regions that should process ignored space. Feature-based evidence extends the same logic: alpha increases in dorsal motion-related regions when motion is irrelevant and in ventral color-related regions when color is irrelevant.
sections.heading: Spatial and Feature Evidence

sections.body: The review argues that alpha gating is not limited to visual spatial orienting. Auditory cues can invoke visual alpha gating, auditory spatial tasks show parietal alpha asymmetries, and tactile attention studies show ipsilateral somatosensory alpha increases. These converging examples support a more general suppressive control process across sensory systems.
sections.heading: Cross-Modal Generality

sections.body: A major alternative is that alpha increases simply mark return to baseline idling while attended regions remain desynchronized. The bilateral rapid-serial presentation design challenges that view because stimulation continues in both hemifields and alpha rises above pre-cue baseline over the ignored stream, making active suppression the stronger interpretation.
sections.heading: Active Suppression Evidence

sections.body: The review connects alpha to behavior by describing correlations between higher pre-stimulus alpha and worse near-threshold detection or discrimination. The causal case is strengthened by rhythmic TMS: 10 Hz stimulation, but not 5 Hz or 20 Hz stimulation, changes visual detection in a spatially specific pattern consistent with alpha-band suppression.
sections.heading: Perceptual Consequences

sections.body: The anatomical account remains cautious. Human TMS and monkey laminar recordings point toward fronto-parietal and cortico-cortical control of task-related alpha, with possible thalamo-cortical involvement. The authors explicitly distinguish attention-related alpha from broader arousal alpha and warn that alpha may differ across cortical areas and behavioral contexts.
sections.heading: Mechanistic Limits

source_dossier.summary_long: This review presents alpha-band activity, roughly 8-14 Hz, as a central mechanism by which selective attention suppresses irrelevant sensory information. The authors distinguish enhancement of attended signals from active suppression of unattended locations, modalities, and features, then focus on the latter. Their main evidential path begins with instructional cueing paradigms: if a cue tells participants to respond only to one modality or location, the uncued stream becomes a true distracter, allowing pre-stimulus alpha changes to be interpreted as preparatory gating rather than simple post-stimulus processing. In intersensory attention, preparing for an auditory target increases parieto-occipital alpha relative to preparing for a visual target, suggesting suppression of visual cortex. In spatial visual attention, alpha increases over occipital regions corresponding to ignored retinotopic space. In feature attention, alpha rises in dorsal or ventral visual-stream sources depending on whether motion or color is irrelevant. The review then broadens the account to auditory and somatosensory spatial attention, where alpha asymmetries also appear over sensory-relevant cortical regions. A key interpretive challenge is whether alpha increases are active suppression or merely passive return to an idling baseline. The authors emphasize evidence from bilateral rapid visual presentation showing alpha above pre-cue baseline over ignored streams while stimulation continues, plus behavioral correlations and rhythmic TMS evidence showing that alpha power and externally driven 10 Hz activity alter perceptual detection. They also discuss anatomical mechanisms, arguing that attention-related alpha is likely controlled mainly by cortico-cortical fronto-parietal networks with possible thalamo-cortical contributions. The account is not presented as fully settled: scalp EEG localization, differences between arousal alpha and task-specific alpha, and mixed effects across cortical layers and areas all limit simple one-mechanism interpretations.
source_dossier.summary_short: Foxe and Snyder argue that alpha-band oscillations are a functional mechanism for suppressing distracting sensory input during selective attention. The review links intersensory, spatial, feature-based, auditory, tactile, TMS, and animal evidence into a common account: alpha power rises in regions processing information that should be ignored.

summary: Foxe and Snyder review converging EEG, TMS, behavioral, and animal evidence that alpha-band oscillations are not merely an idling rhythm but can be deployed as an active mechanism for suppressing irrelevant sensory information during selective attention.

warnings.message: The source is a review article; several claims synthesize cited studies rather than reporting one new primary experiment.
The extracted markdown preserves two-column PDF text on shared lines; evidence was interpreted conservatively from readable passages and figure captions.
